explanation:
## One pass, three counters

```cpp
int less{};
int equal{};
int greater{};
for (int x : v)
{
    if (x < target)       ++less;
    else if (x == target) ++equal;
    else                  ++greater;
}
```

The three counters are declared **inside** the per-query loop, so each query
starts from zero. Declaring them above that loop is the commonest bug here: the
first query is right, and every one after it includes the previous totals. The
invariant catches it on the second line of output, where reading the numbers
would not.

## The invariant

```
less + equal + greater == n
```

This holds after every pass of the inner loop, with `n` replaced by "elements
seen so far" - which is what makes it an invariant rather than just a fact about
the answer. It is true because the three conditions **partition** the integers:

```
    x < target        x == target        x > target
  <-------------|         |         |------------->
                      exactly one of these holds, for every x
```

Exhaustive, because every integer is below, equal to or above any other. Non
overlapping, because no integer is both below and equal.

That gives a free test. In real code it would be written down:

```cpp
#include <cassert>
assert(less + equal + greater == static_cast<int>(v.size()));
```

An `assert` compiled out of release builds costs nothing in production and
catches the mistake the moment it happens in testing - which beats discovering
it three functions later from a wrong total.

## Why the `else` chain, and where `<=` goes wrong

With an else-if chain, the second test only runs when the first was false, so
`x == target` is reached only for values not below the target. The final `else`
needs no condition at all: anything neither below nor equal must be above.

Three independent `if`s happen to work here, since the conditions are mutually
exclusive on their own. But they are fragile in a way the chain is not. Write
this:

```cpp
if (x <= target) ++less;        // off by one case
if (x == target) ++equal;
if (x > target)  ++greater;
```

and every element equal to the target is counted twice - once as `less`, once as
`equal`. The output still *looks* reasonable: the numbers are all plausible, the
ordering is plausible, and only the total gives it away. `6 less 3 equal 3
greater 2` sums to 8 for an array of 6, which is impossible.

The general point: when conditions are meant to be exclusive, write them in a
form where the compiler and the structure enforce it, rather than one where
exclusivity is a property you have to keep checking.

## What the library offers

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
auto less    = std::count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [&](int x) { return x < target; });
auto equal   = std::count(v.begin(), v.end(), target);
auto greater = std::count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [&](int x) { return x > target; });
```

Three named operations, each obviously correct, and three separate passes over
the data. For 2000 elements that is irrelevant; for a few million it is three
times the memory traffic to answer one question.

`std::count` returns `std::iterator_traits<...>::difference_type`, which is a
signed 64-bit type on most platforms - hence `auto` rather than `int`, and
another case where the library hands back a wider type than you expected.

## Faster, if the data were sorted

Every one of these counts is a position in a sorted array:

```
less    = lower_bound(target) - begin()
equal   = upper_bound(target) - lower_bound(target)
greater = end() - upper_bound(target)
```

which is two binary searches - O(log n) per query instead of O(n), after one
O(n log n) sort. For `q` queries that turns O(n*q) into O((n + q) log n), and for
n = q = 200000 it is the difference between forty billion operations and about
seven million.

That is the next problem in this sequence. Here the data is deliberately
unsorted, so that the linear version is the correct answer and the comparison is
honest rather than hypothetical.
